title: 3-Read Friday #41: A New Book, Coaching Rehearsal, and Interdependencies
author: Craig Barton
summary: In this edition of 3-Read Friday, Craig Barton curates three posts loosely tied together by the theme of how expertise actually spreads and sticks in a school. The first, from the blogger G-Rob, reviews Hector Ruiz Martin's book How Do We Learn, which Barton picked up after Doug Lemov recommended it at a CPD session; Barton highlights the book's treatment of prior knowledge as the hook that sent it onto his summer reading list. The second, from Paul Cline, interrogates instructional coaching's reliance on rehearsal, including Cline's own admission that he sometimes skips it, a point Barton flags as valuable for leaders, coaches, and coachees alike. The third, from Matthew Evans, argues that an individual teacher's practice is never really individual: its impact is shaped by the interdependent behaviour of every other teacher in the building, a dynamic Barton connects to his own habit of meeting with SLT whenever he works with a maths department. Together the three picks move from what to teach, to how to coach it, to why school-wide buy-in determines whether either sticks.
points: Barton frames rehearsal in coaching as valuable but not sacrosanct, endorsing Cline's willingness to sometimes skip it depending on context.
He connects Evans's interdependency argument to his own consulting practice of always looping in SLT so departmental change has structural support.
He treats a book recommendation (How Do We Learn) passed along from Doug Lemov's CPD session as reason enough to prioritise it for summer reading.
The throughline across all three picks is that individual technique (a coaching move, a lesson idea) only works within a wider system of colleagues and leadership.
quotes: I attended some CPD delivered by Doug Lemov last week (#namedrop).
He shared a passage from the book about the importance of building on prior knowledge, and I was hooked, so it is straight on my summer reading list.
The bit that really stood out for me was the section on rehearsal and Paul's confession that sometimes he chooses not to include rehearsal as part of his coaching.
There is plenty to think about for leaders, coaches and coachees here.
When I visit a school to work with their maths department, I always insist on meeting with SLT members at the end of the day to discuss what I have asked colleagues to work on.
It is much easier for a department to make a change if there is support from SLT, but also if other departments might wish to work in the same area.
Matthew's superb post articulates the power of such interdependencies.
